title: bash and zsh: two shells, one language
summary: zsh reads almost every bash line the same way. Learn the few places where it doesn't, and why scripts name their shell.

scheme: zsh                  the shell you type in
#!/usr/bin/env bash  first line of a script:
text: Your terminal runs a shell: often bash on Linux, zsh on a Mac and for many developers. Both read the same commands, pipes, quotes and loops, so what Bashou teaches works in both.
- A script names its shell on its first line: #!/usr/bin/env bash. When you run it as ./script.sh, bash runs it, even from zsh, so it behaves the same for everyone.
- echo $0 shows the shell you're typing in right now (a leading - just means a login shell).
bash splits the value of a variable at its spaces: $f becomes two words, and ls looks for two files. zsh doesn't split it, so the same line works there.
- Write "$f" with quotes: it is one word in both shells, and it keeps working when your script runs in bash.

scheme: bash: ls gets *.pdf as it is
text: When no file matches a pattern, bash gives the pattern itself to the command, and zsh stops the line with an error. Either way, nothing matched.
- zsh and bash match * and ? the same way, so look with ls first: the list you see is what rm would get.
A list (an array) keeps several values in one variable. bash numbers its items from 0, zsh from 1: ${colors[1]} is the second color in bash and the first one in zsh.
- In a script that starts with #!/usr/bin/env bash, count from 0: bash runs it.
- ${colors[@]} gives all the items, the same way in both shells.
